articles.title: Report: Eight US Marines wounded in Iranian strike near Strait of Hormuz
articles.body:
Report: Eight US Marines wounded in Iranian strike near Strait of Hormuz
TEHRAN — An Iranian anti-ship cruise missile strike in the Strait of Hormuz has left at least eight US Marines wounded, exposing the mounting operational vulnerabilities of the American military presence in West Asia and puncturing Washington’s carefully curated narrative of naval dominance in the Persian Gulf.
The high-precision strike, which occurred on September 14, targeted an unauthorized maritime vessel deployed within the strategic chokepoint. According to disclosures from American officials, the impact resulted in immediate trauma among the personnel on board, including smoke inhalation and symptoms consistent with traumatic brain injury (TBI) and severe concussions. The injured troops—comprising seven enlisted service members and one officer—were attached to an expeditionary battalion landing team operating covertly aboard a non-naval, commercial-grade maritime vessel rather than a standard commissioned warship.
The incident, concealed by the United States Department of War for nearly two weeks, came to light only after the Pentagon’s Defense Casualty Analysis System (DCAS) belatedly added the wounded Marines to its casualty rosters for Overseas Operations, without disclosing the time, location, or circumstances of the engagement. Both US Central Command (CENTCOM) and the Pentagon declined to formally address the strike, extending a pattern of information suppression and data manipulation that has characterized Washington’s public disclosures since the outbreak of hostilities in late February.
The successful missile engagement serves as a potent reminder of Iran’s comprehensive operational control over the Strait of Hormuz and adjacent littoral waters. Operating under strict rules of engagement, naval units of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) and the Army have established absolute surveillance over the waterway, through which a significant portion of global petroleum supplies must transit.
Tehran has reiterated that maritime security in the Strait of Hormuz is indivisible and sovereign. Hostile military assets and non-authorized vessels attempting illegal passage, espionage, or the enforcement of unilateral Western blockades against Iranian commerce are treated as legitimate tactical targets. Military authorities in Tehran have repeatedly cautioned foreign powers that any vessel defying Iranian navigational regulations, failing to transmit required identification, or participating in hostile maneuvers will be intercepted or neutralized without hesitation.
Despite Washington’s deployment of vast naval assets to the region—including more than 50,000 personnel, multiple carrier strike groups led by the USS George Washington and the USS George H.W. Bush, and accompanying guided-missile escorts—the Pentagon’s attempt to impose an unlawful blockade on Iranian ports has been systematically frustrated. Iranian coastal defense batteries, armed with advanced radar systems and indigenous anti-ship cruise and ballistic missiles, hold every foreign vessel in the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman within immediate targeting range.
US casualties and information blackout
The September 14 strike has renewed scrutiny over the Pentagon’s opaque reporting practices regarding military casualties. Since the United States and Israel jointly launched their aggressive, unprovoked war against Iran on February 28, defense analysts and regional observers have noted an unprecedented level of discrepancy and confusion in official American reports.
While DCAS records show that well over 860 US military personnel have sustained injuries since the start of the conflict, independent observers argue the true figures are substantially higher. Over the summer, the Pentagon abruptly reclassified its casualty methodologies, retroactively lowering official death counts and categorizing combat casualties under vague bureaucratic labels to soften the domestic political impact of the campaign’s escalating human toll. The delayed logging of the eight Marines—justified retroactively by US officials as a standard administrative reporting lag—reflects a broader strategy aimed at downplaying the efficacy of Iranian defensive countermeasures.
Furthermore, the deployment of combat troops aboard an undisclosed “maritime vessel” points to a growing operational shift by CENTCOM. Facing devastating losses and heightened risk to major surface combatants from Iran’s asymmetric swarming tactics, naval drones, and precision coastal batteries, the US military has increasingly resorted to utilizing auxiliary, commercial, or unmarked hulls to evade detection—a strategy that Iranian intelligence and surveillance networks continue to successfully penetrate and neutralize.
Iran’s non-negotiable terms
Iranian political leadership and top military commanders have made it explicitly clear that safe, uninterrupted transit through the Strait of Hormuz remains entirely contingent upon the United States acknowledging regional geopolitical realities and complying with Iran’s legitimate terms.
Tehran has outlined a clear path for the normalization of maritime traffic in the waterway: Washington must bring an immediate, unconditional, and permanent end to the war of aggression it initiated on February 28 alongside Israel. Iranian officials emphasize that no foreign power will be permitted to enforce a state of economic strangulation against the Iranian people while simultaneously demanding unrestricted access for its own war fleet and commercial shipping through Iran’s front yard.
More broadly, senior officials in Tehran have repeatedly affirmed that enduring peace and stability in West Asia and the Persian Gulf can never be achieved under the shadow of foreign occupation. The root cause of regional friction, Iranian authorities insist, remains the destabilizing footprint of extra-regional forces. Real security is attainable only through collective regional cooperation among Persian Gulf littoral states, predicated on the complete, comprehensive, and irreversible expulsion of all American military personnel, bases, and hardware from the region.
As long as the United States continues to pursue a reckless militaristic agenda, sponsor Israeli aggression, and trespass upon Iranian territorial jurisdiction, Tehran has pledged that its armed forces will vigorously exercise their legitimate right to self-defense, ensuring that every act of adventurism in the waters of the Persian Gulf is met with a swift, decisive, and punitive response.

articles.title: Zelenskyy Warns of New Russian Mobilization and 10,000 North Korean Troop Deployment
articles.body:
The death toll from Russia’s jet-powered drone attacks mounted in Ukraine while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned that the Kremlin is preparing for a new troop mobilization at home and a fresh deployment of 10,000 North Korean soldiers.
After Zelenskyy spoke, journalists in the Ukrainian capital reported explosions in the city during a missile alert early on September 29. Details were not immediately available.
On September 28, at least two people were killed when a drone hit the National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv amid some of the most relentless aerial strikes -- often with new jet-powered drones -- on the Ukrainian capital since the start of the full-scale war in February 2022.
Zelenskyy said at least nine people had been killed and more than 80 injured in Russian drone strikes throughout the country during the day.
In his nightly video address, Zelenskyy said Ukraine was struggling to counter the high-flying Russian jet-powered drones, with the interception rate of just below 60 percent. He said 90 of the 120 drones fired on Ukraine were jet-powered, as opposed to propeller-driven.
“New interceptors are being actively tested," he said in his address.
"Some combat groups are using them, but, of course, some details still need to be refined to achieve enough effectiveness and scale. We are speeding up the developers.”
Zelenskyy also cited a report from Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, that he said showed that Russia had launched a new wave of mobilization for its military.
"They are increasing the number of people they recruit through various methods," he said. "It is important that the governments of countries from which Russia recruits people for its army take action against this."
Preparations Under Way, Zelenskyy Says
Zelenskyy said some 8,000 North Korean troops, brought in by the Kremlin in 2024 to counter a Ukrainian incursion into Russia’s Kursk region, remained in the country and that preparations were under way for the deployment of a further 10,000 soldiers.
Zelenskyy said in a post on social media that the North Koreans -- who reportedly suffered heavy losses during the previous deployment -- were "being selected for training and subsequent deployment to Russia."
Russian President Vladimir Putin has rejected reports of a new mobilization as "utter nonsense," although he did on September 28 sign a decree increasing the size of the army by 15,500 troops -- the fourth such order this year.
"The authorized personnel strength of the Russian armed forces is to be set at 2,441,630 units, including 1,550,500 military personnel," the decree said, giving no reason for the addition.
Russia has suffered massive losses to soldiers, weapons, and military hardware since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, a venture the Kremlin reportedly believed would take only a few weeks to end in victory.
Putin last ordered a mobilization of reservists in 2022, and another such move would likely prove highly unpopular with the Russian population.
Difficult Reforms
Meanwhile, Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskiy warned that the public finances situation “remains difficult,” saying the slow pace of reforms has caused Western partners to hold up financial commitment.
“Part of the planned international funding has not yet arrived. In particular, due to the fact that Ukraine has not had time to fulfill some of the obligations it has undertaken to international partners,” without providing details.
Koretskiy has urged Ukrainian lawmakers to pass difficult reforms, including taxation of postal packages from abroad and a comprehensive overhaul of the taxation system.
Zelenskyy said he had held meetings on September 28 with Koretskiy and other officials to discuss “our key priorities in working with partners over the coming weeks in response to this situation. “
“The government, for its part, is doing everything necessary to fulfill its commitments and receive planned international funding. We are working together with the parliament. And here, responsible work from deputies of all factions and groups is important,” he added, although he did not cite specifics.

articles.title: Defense Intelligence of Ukraine Strikes Russian L-39 Aircraft, Three Boats, and Multiple Radar Systems
articles.body:
Operators of the Prymary special unit of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine struck a number of enemy military targets, including in Crimea.
The Defense Intelligence of Ukraine published footage of the operation on its social media pages.
During the operation, the intelligence officers struck a railway bridge over the North Crimean Canal, which Russian occupation forces use to provide logistical support to their units.
In addition, the unit destroyed nine communications and surveillance facilities, including communications towers, electronic warfare (EW) and electronic intelligence (ELINT) systems, airborne radar stations, and MESH repeaters that provide secure wireless communications between Russian units.
The Prymary unit struck a Nebo-U radar designed to detect and track airborne targets. The system can detect fighter aircraft at ranges up to 400 km at altitudes of 20 km, as well as ballistic missiles at distances up to 300 km and altitudes up to 50 km.
The special forces also struck the command post of a mobile two-coordinate P-18 Terek radar. The station operates in the meter-wave band and can detect airborne targets at ranges of up to 360 km and altitudes of up to 27 km, and can provide target designation to surface-to-air missile systems.
Two 39N6E Kasta-2E radars were also hit. This low-altitude, decimeter-band radar can detect aircraft, helicopters, and cruise missiles flying as low as 100 meters, at ranges up to 42 km. At higher altitudes, its detection range extends to up to 150 km.
Among the adversary’s aviation losses was an L-39 Albatros jet trainer/light attack aircraft. The aircraft has a maximum takeoff weight of 4.7 tonnes, a maximum speed of 750 km/h, a practical flight range of up to 1,100 km, and a weapons payload of up to 250 kg carried on external hardpoints.
At sea, the personnel of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine engaged a BK-10 high-speed assault craft. The 10.4-meter vessel has a maximum speed of up to 40 knots, a range of up to 400 nautical miles, and a troop-carrying capacity of up to nine personnel.
Another maritime target was a BK-16 high-speed transport-and-assault craft. 16.4 meters long and displacing 19.5 tonnes, the vessel can reach speeds of up to 45 knots, has a range of up to 400 nautical miles, and can transport 19 troops in addition to a two-person crew.
In addition, the personnel of the Defense Intelligence of Ukraine destroyed a Project 12150 Mongoose high-speed patrol craft. With a displacement of 27.2 tonnes and a length of 19.45 meters, the vessel can reach speeds of up to 50 knots and has an endurance of up to two days, with a maximum range of up to 410 nautical miles.
On September 28, unmanned aerial vehicles attacked railway infrastructure in several areas of Russia’s Bryansk and Kaluga regions.

articles.title: Russia Pounds Kyiv Again With Ballistic Missiles Hours After Attacks Kill 2, Injure 26
articles.body:
Russia launched a fresh ballistic missile attack on Kyiv early Tuesday, hours after a day-long barrage killed two people and injured 26 across the Ukrainian capital.
Several loud explosions rang out across Kyiv early hours of Tuesday, Sept. 29, as air defenses activated during a new air raid alert.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“New ballistic missiles are heading towards Kyiv,” Ukraine’s Air Force warned on Telegram as the attack unfolded.
Ukrainian monitoring reports said the new assault began at around 1:20 a.m., with warnings of ballistic missile launches from Russia’s Kursk region as Kyiv again came under missile threat.
The renewed attack came only hours after Kyiv endured waves of Russian strikes throughout Monday, Sept. 28, hitting multiple districts and leaving civilian buildings burning across the capital.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said late Monday that two people had been killed and 26 others injured, including three children. Eight of the wounded were hospitalized and one remained in serious condition.
One of the dead was initially reported after a Russian drone struck a non-residential building belonging to Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv’s historic center.
Rescuers later recovered the body of a second victim from the building during emergency operations.
Russian attacks were reported across the Shevchenkivskyi, Obolonskyi, Solomianskyi, Darnytskyi, Podilskyi and other districts during the day.
Russia to Begin Additional Mobilization, Expand North Korean Troop Presence
In central Kyiv, a strike set part of the National Academy of Sciences building ablaze. Another strike hit a seven-story building housing a Dobrobut medical facility, where seven people were reported injured, six of them employees.
Russia also struck the Darnytsia pharmaceutical plant, while fires and damage were reported at other non-residential and commercial buildings around the capital.
Klitschko continued reporting fresh impacts into Monday evening. A non-residential building in Obolonskyi district was struck more than once, vehicles caught fire after a drone fell into a residential courtyard in Solomianskyi district, and a three-story business center was hit in Sviatoshynskyi district.
President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned Monday’s strikes and said Russia would face consequences.
“Every Russian terrorist attack results in casualties that could have been prevented had the pressure on Russia finally become total,” he said, calling for stronger international action against those financing and producing Russia’s weapons.
Ukraine’s Air Force said Russia launched 124 drones during Monday’s attacks, including 86 jet-powered UAVs, and reported that 86 aerial targets were destroyed or suppressed.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Putin orders army expansion as Zelenskyy says more North Koreans to be deployed in Russia
articles.body:
- 
  Russian president Vladimir Putin has ordered an increase in the size of the army to 1.55 million active servicemen, according to a presidential decree on Monday. The order comes as both Russia and Ukraine suffer mounting casualties in the more than four-and-a-half-year Ukraine war. The expansion, which follows a similar increase ordered in August, will put the size of Russia’s armed forces at 2,441,630. Of those are 1,550,000 active servicemen, an increase of 15,500.
- 
  Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X on Monday there were now more than 8,000 North Korean troops on Russian territory and preparations were under way to deploy another 10,000 troops. Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong-un confirmed for the first time last year that North Korea had sent troops to fight for Russia in the war with Ukraine, with both leaders describing the soldiers as “heroes”.
- 
  Citing “new data” on the deployment of North Korean troops to Russia, Zelenskyy said they were “being selected for training and subsequent deployment to Russia”. North Korea has sent an estimated 14,000 to 15,000 troops to support Russia’s war in Ukraine since 2024, according to Ukrainian and South Korean estimates, with most deployed in the Kursk region to help repel a Ukrainian incursion.
- 
  Explosions were heard in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv early on Tuesday, a Reuters witness said, as Russia continues its near-daily attacks. Missile debris fell in the courtyard of a residential building, among other damage, and a non-residential building caught fire in another part of the city, Kyiv mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. On Monday, Zelenskyy said nine people had been killed and more than 80 injured in Russian drone strikes throughout the country, including in Kyiv.
- 
  Pope Leo urged Russia and Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end their war, hours after he had urged European leaders seeking to end conflicts to make concessions to achieve peace. Addressing a press conference aboard his flight to Rome on Monday after a four-day trip to France, Leo said the 1.4-billion-member Catholic church had an obligation to call for peace and respect of human life. “The Church has a responsibility to promote these values, continually inviting leaders – from Russia and Ukraine, as well as other countries – to come together, sit down, engage in dialogue,” the pope said.
- 
  Nato’s top military commander said Russia’s sabotage campaign in Europe was failing to put countries off supporting Ukraine. “State-directed sabotage is growing increasingly brazen,” US general Alexus Grynkewich told a committee of EU lawmakers on Monday. Nato’s supreme allied commander for Europe cited recent incidents including the discovery of an explosive-laden drone at a German airport and a Russian naval ship firing flares at a Danish helicopter. “These are clear examples of attempts to instil fear and fracture our unified support to Ukraine. It isn’t working,” he said.
- 
  Ukraine will postpone some spending commitments, including reconstruction work, because of delays in receiving aid from its foreign backers, Ukraine’s prime minister said. The government would carry out these projects eventually, “but for now, all resources must be directed toward critical areas”, Sergiy Koretsky said on Telegram on Monday. Russia’s offensive has battered Ukraine’s economy, causing billions of dollars in destruction and punching a huge hole in its neighbour’s finances.
- 
  Putin has ordered the Russian assets of German retailer Metro AG to be placed under temporary administration, amid Russian-German tensions over the Ukraine war. The order, posted on Monday on the government website, did not state a reason. The step follows similar steps against the Russia businesses of global food company Nestlé and French retailer Auchan under a 2023 decree aimed at businesses associated with “unfriendly countries”. Temporary administration has led to local owners taking over the Russia businesses of French dairy concern Danone and Danish brewer Carlsberg at knockdown prices.
- 
  A Russian jet-powered drone struck a Ukrainian village near the Polish border earlier on Monday, damaging a border checkpoint, a regional Ukrainian official said. The official did not give details about the nature of the checkpoint or extent of damage from the blast. Russia has launched multiple attacks near Ukraine’s border with Poland in recent weeks, drawing condemnation from Warsaw and its European allies.

articles.title: Iran says it's up to Trump to choose between war and diplomacy
articles.body:
Live Updates: Iran says Trump must choose between war or diplomacy as talks resume
What to know about the Iran war today:
- President Trump confirmed that American and Iranian negotiators exchanged messages through mediators on Monday. He didn't share any details on the talks, but said, "We're going to win."
- Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran is "fully prepared for the war to be resumed," and also for the possibility of renewed diplomacy aimed at ending the seven-month conflict. It's "up to President Trump to choose," he said.
- Last week, Iran proposed a seven-day ceasefire and the phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, contingent upon the U.S. meeting conditions laid out in the mid-June memorandum of understanding, which fell apart after several weeks. Mr. Trump publicly rejected the new Iranian proposal last week, and Iran has insisted it will not change its demands.
On Iran talks, Trump says "I offered them NOTHING"
President Trump denied that he has offered to relieve Iran of some sanctions and unfreeze its funds, writing on Truth Social: "I offered them NOTHING!"
The president was reacting to an Axios story that said Mr. Trump is open to granting sanctions relief in exchange for progress on Iran's nuclear program.
A U.S. official also told CBS News on Monday that Mr. Trump is willing to grant Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds if progress is made on the nuclear issue.
Trump confirms U.S. spoke to Iranian negotiators through mediators today
President Trump confirmed to reporters that American and Iranian negotiators exchanged messages through mediators on Monday.
He did not share any details on the talks, saying, "We're going to win."
CBS News reported earlier Monday that indirect U.S.-Iran talks began in the morning. A U.S. official said Mr. Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds if there is concrete progress on Iran's nuclear program, but there will not be a deal unless the nuclear issues are addressed, and the two sides remain apart on the timing of commitments.
An Iranian diplomatic source told CBS News the primary issue is that the U.S. president does not seem to have a clear position on what he wants from negotiations, making it difficult to move from discussions to a concrete agreement.
Uncertainty about Strait of Hormuz weighs on U.S. bond market
Yields in the U.S. bond market cranked higher Monday and again reached their highest levels in roughly two decades, which knocked U.S. stocks further from their record high.
Monday's rise in yields followed the latest swings for oil prices, which have been yo-yoing on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow tankers to flow freely again through the Strait of Hormuz and deliver oil from the Middle East to customers worldwide.
The latest turns came after President Trump said over the weekend he's rejecting an offer from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program.
Gas prices could soar if the U.S. bans diesel exports, economists say
A move by the U.S. to temporarily halt diesel exports amid record-high prices would initially lower costs, but a prolonged ban could drive up domestic gasoline prices, according to Goldman Sachs.
President Trump on Sunday told reporters his administration is "very seriously" considering a ban on diesel exports. Calls to restrict exports of U.S.-refined diesel have picked up in recent weeks, mostly from Republican lawmakers, as a lever they believe will help lower prices. Diesel hit a record $6.53 a gallon on Sept. 22, and has only eased slightly since then, slipping to $6.45 a gallon on Monday, according to AAA data.
The war with Iran is pushing up oil and gas prices, creating widespread financial strain on U.S. motorists, food delivery drivers and farmers.
Read more here.
 
Yemen says it launched over 350 strikes against Houthi targets
Yemen's defense ministry said it carried out 356 strikes against Houthi military targets over the past 24 hours, killing or wounding an estimated 476 fighters.
Video posted by the Yemeni military showed strikes on various Houthi positions across several front lines.
Military spokesman Col. Majed al-Nazili said the strikes targeted Houthi command centers, weapons depots, artillery positions, vehicles and other military equipment.
 
U.S. official: Talks ongoing through mediators, but no deal unless nuclear issue addressed
The U.S. and Iran are continuing to have discussions, viewed as positive and constructive, through mediators, but there will not be a deal unless the nuclear issues are addressed, according to a U.S. official.
President Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds if there is concrete progress on nuclear issues, the official said. Iran has indicated it is flexible on nuclear issues, but the two sides still remain apart on the timing of commitments and who takes which steps first.
The official said the U.S. is skeptical of Iran's promises after it broke the memorandum of understanding by firing on commercial vessels, and is looking for assurances that Iran is serious.
Iranians face arduous journeys as U.S. sanctions ground planes
Flying out of Iran has long required patience in the face of restrictions and delays, but new U.S. sanctions have grounded flights on short notice and left war-weary travelers feeling trapped as they try to leave the country.
Passengers who booked tickets out of Iran to Middle Eastern destinations like the United Arab Emirates, Iraq, Oman and Turkey have faced short-notice cancellations as the latest sanctions bite.
Among those scrambling for a way out is Mitra, a 49-year-old woman who had planned to travel to Paris via Istanbul along with her brother, but who now faces a long journey by road to get to Turkey.
"Some airlines are still selling tickets, but they keep getting canceled. It honestly makes us feel completely trapped," she told an AFP journalist in Paris, using a pseudonym for fear of retribution by authorities.
"When we were told that flights had been suspended, we decided to travel to Istanbul by land instead," she said.
Mitra described paying around $75 to book a flight to the Iranian city of Tabriz, from where she will travel by road for several hours to reach the border.
In Van in Turkey, they will stay at a hotel, because the wait at the border can be long and chaotic.
"At this point, we're just hoping that we can actually get out. They might even close the land border," she fears.
Israel releases on bail U.S.-Palestinian reporter accused of working for Iran
An Israeli court on Monday released on bail a Palestinian-American journalist who had been detained for nearly two weeks on charges including working for Iran, her lawyer told the AFP news agency.
An AFP journalist saw Naqaa Hamed, who has contributed to Iran's state-run Press TV, being released at a checkpoint near Jenin in the Israeli-occupied West Bank.
Hamed's lawyer Khaled Mahajneh told AFP that an Israeli military court released her on bail of 8,000 shekels — about $2,600 — and on condition she comply with future summons for questioning.
Mahajneh said Hamed spent "two weeks of detention under difficult conditions at Damon prison" in the northern Israeli city of Haifa.
The Israeli military arrested Hamed on Sept. 15 at a checkpoint near Bethlehem as she was returning from a reporting assignment for Turkish broadcaster TRT, according to her family and a journalist who was accompanying her at the time.
Press TV, which is owned by the Iranian state, reported on her arrest and release and described her as its West Bank correspondent.
Colleagues said Hamed, who holds U.S. citizenship, had stopped working with Press TV about a month earlier and had become a freelance journalist.
The Israeli government considers Press TV a propaganda arm of Iran's government.
Israel is currently holding 36 journalists in its prisons, according to the Palestinian Prisoners' Club, an NGO working for prisoners' rights.
Rising oil prices push U.S. stock values down as Trump rejects Iran's latest offer
Rising oil prices are knocking the U.S. stock market further from its record high on Monday, while building pressure even higher within the U.S. bond market.
The S&P 500 fell 0.8% and gave back most of its gains from last week, which had brought it to the brink of its all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 372 points, or 0.7%, as of 11:45 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was 1% lower.
Most of the U.S. stock market sank under the weight of a 2.8% rise for the most actively traded contract in the market for Brent crude oil to $100.19 per barrel. That overshadowed a gain for Wall Street's most influential stock, Nvidia, after it announced a historic funneling of cash to its investors through a buyback of its shares.
Oil prices have been yo-yoing on uncertainty about when the war with Iran will allow tankers to flow freely again through the Strait of Hormuz and deliver oil from the Middle East to customers worldwide. The latest turns came after President Donald Trump said over the weekend he's rejecting an offer from Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program.
"I'd like to make a deal, too," Mr. Trump said Saturday. "But that deal would not be acceptable."
Brent climbed above $101 per barrel Monday morning, before the U.S. stock market opened for trading, but it pared its gains as U.S. officials said mediators were still working with Iran and the United States on a deal to end the fighting and open the strait.
For all its ups and downs, a barrel of Brent remains much higher than the roughly $72 it cost before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran in late February. That has helped worsen inflation, and the average price for a gallon of regular gasoline is up to nearly $4.48 from $3.13 a year ago, according to AAA.
Iranian foreign minister to meet mediators in New York over potential renewal of talks with U.S.
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi is scheduled to meet mediators in New York on Monday morning to discuss the latest proposals and efforts to revive negotiations with the United States, Iran's semi-official ISNA news agency reported.
According to ISNA, Iran has proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz as part of a deal to end the war, in exchange for the release of Iranian funds and assets that Tehran says have been unlawfully blocked.
The proposal was conveyed to the U.S. through mediators in New York. Although President Trump rejected the offer over the weekend, Iranian officials say indirect contacts and mediation efforts continue.
Araghchi said Iran is awaiting a response via the mediators before deciding its next steps. He reiterated that any move toward reopening the Strait of Hormuz would depend on Iran's conditions being met, saying Tehran would not back down from its conditions.
"We are waiting for the definitive opinions to be conveyed to us by the mediators and we will make a decision based on that," ISNA quoted Araghchi as saying.
No representatives from the U.S. side will be attending Monday's meeting, the report said.

U.K. police release on bail 5 men arrested near air base used by U.S. for Iran strikes
British counter terror police released on bail five British men arrested over the weekend near a Royal Air Force base used by U.S. forces to launch strikes on Iran.
Metropolitan Police Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor, head of Counter Terrorism Policing, said the men were being released following "extensive interviews," adding that the investigation was not over and they remained "subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others."
Referring to reports that British authorities were investigating a possible link to Iran, he said: "I know there is significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident."
"At this stage we are keeping an open mind in this investigation … be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle. Including that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state."
Iran said Monday that it "categorically denies" any involvement in the incident.
Iran "categorically rejects" involvement in suspected terror plot on military base hosting U.S. aircraft
Iran "categorically rejects" claims that it was involved in a suspected terror plot on a British military base hosting U.S. aircraft, its embassy in London said Monday.
British counterterrorism police were leading an investigation Monday after five men were arrested on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act in an English village near a Royal Air Force base used by U.S. bombers.
The Associated Press reported that British authorities are investigating the possibility of a link between Iran and the arrests near RAF Fairford, but that as of Monday there had been no conclusions reached about whether the apparent plot against the base could have been state-backed.
This year, groups with purported links to Iran have carried out several attacks on U.K. soil, primarily targeting the Jewish community in north London.
U.S. and Iran expected to continue talking this week through mediators, official tells Reuters
The U.S. and Iran are expected to have separate talks with mediators on Monday or Tuesday, an official with knowledge of the negotiations told the Reuters news agency.
With Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in the U.S., as well as Qatari mediators, the talks are set to focus on an updated version of the seven-day proposal Iran gave to U.S. counterparts last week during the United Nations General Assembly, the official told Reuters.
President Trump said Sunday that he expected talks with Iran to resume in the coming days, a day after he rejected a new proposal put forward by Tehran last week for a seven-day ceasefire and phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Mr. Trump told Axios. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."
Saudi Arabia's strategic East-West Crude Oil Pipeline operational again, Bloomberg says
Saudi Arabia has resumed exporting oil using its crucial East-West Crude Oil Pipeline after drone strikes earlier this month forced it shut, according to a source with direct knowledge of the matter quoted by Bloomberg.
Saudi Arabia had been using the pipeline to transport oil from its eastern production hubs to its Red Sea ports for export — a vital alternative route as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has remained severely disrupted by the U.S.-Iran war.
The pipeline was shut down earlier this month after a series of drone attacks that Saudi authorities blamed on Iran-backed militias in Iraq.
The state-run energy giant Saudi Aramco, which operates the kingdom's oil infrastructure, tested the pipeline last week and has now resumed overseas shipments via the Red Sea route, a source familiar with the operation told Bloomberg.
Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen have vowed to impose a blockade of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea ports and against Saudi ships, and they have targeted several vessels in the region.
Iran lodges complaint with U.N. over U.S. sanctions on its aviation industry
Iran has lodged a complaint with the United Nations over U.S. sanctions against its aviation sector, which have forced the cancellation of many flights across the region, state media reported Monday.
The U.S. imposed restrictions this month on the entire Iranian aviation industry and vowed to take a hard line against any companies or countries that continue to assist it.
As the sanctions took effect last Wednesday, some major airlines were forced to cancel international flights as several nations in the region implemented bans.
"To defend the legitimate rights of the aviation industry and counter illegal restrictions imposed by America, Iran has drafted and submitted a formal protest to the International Civil Aviation Organisation (ICAO)," said civil aviation chief Abouzar Shiroudi, according to Iran's official IRNA news agency.
CBS/AFP
Ayatollah Khamenei says U.S. forces will soon be pushed back
Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei has been quoted as predicting that U.S. military forces will soon be driven out of the Arabian Sea.
In a message to mark Iran's Sacred Defense Week, the ayatollah — who has not been seen or heard from directly since the war began — said U.S. forces were unable to advance beyond the Arabian Sea, which leads to the Strait of Hormuz, "because of the painful blows they have received."
He added that soon, U.S. troops would be driven from the Arabian Sea, too.
U.S. forces have operated across the region since the war began, including to escort commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz in defiance of Iran's bid to control traffic through the vital waterway.
The wide-ranging message attributed by Iranian state media to Khamenei included praise for Iran's military forces, as well as for the former leader of the Iran-backed Hezbollah group in Lebanon.
Khamenei was named Iran's new supreme leader soon after his father and predecessor, Ali Khamenei, was killed in the first round of U.S.-Israeli strikes, which sparked the war on Feb. 28.
The younger Khamenei has not been seen, even in video, since he was named the supreme leader, and senior U.S. officials have said he was likely seriously wounded in the same strike that killed his father.
Value of Iran's currency falls to all-time low against the dollar
The Iranian rial has fallen to a new historic low against the U.S. dollar, with the free-market selling rate surpassing 2.4 million rials per dollar on Monday.
Data from Pashizi, which tracks Iran's free-market exchange rates, put the dollar at around 2.4 million rials as Iran faces high inflation, sweeping sanctions and growing disruption to foreign trade.
Annual inflation has reached 61.4% in August, while food prices are reported to have risen 128% from a year earlier, according to data from Iran's Statistical Center.
Iran's U.N. delegation has no plans to negotiate directly with the U.S.
Iranian state media said Monday that Iran's delegation at the U.N. General Assembly in New York had no plans to hold direct talks with the U.S., after President Trump said he expected more negotiations to take place this week.
"Iran's delegation in New York has no plans for negotiations with the United States," said the official IRNA news agency, citing an unnamed source close to the group.
Mr. Trump told Axios on Sunday he expected negotiations to continue this week, and added that the Iranian leaders were interested in reaching an agreement because they are "losing badly."
"Iran's views and positions were conveyed clearly and explicitly to the U.S. side ... via a Qatari mediator," IRNA said, adding that the Iranian delegation would return to Tehran on Tuesday.
Since the outbreak of the war in February, negotiations between Tehran and Washington have occurred largely through mediators.
CBS/AFP
British police investigating possible Iranian links to suspected terrorist plot against U.K. air base used by U.S.
U.K. police said five men arrested in the early hours of Sunday near an air base used by the United States during its war against Iran were being held on suspicion of preparing a terrorist act that appeared to involve three trucks.
RAF Fairford, a U.K. Royal Air Force base about 85 miles west of London in rural Gloucestershire, has been used by American bombers to conduct strikes against Iranian missile sites. The British government, under an agreement made under former Prime Minister Keir Starmer, granted the U.S. permission to use Farford and other key U.K. bases provided it was only for strikes defined as defensive in nature.
Authorities are investigating a link between the arrests in Fairford and Iran as one possibility. Iranian authorities have declared all bases used to attack Iranian territory as legitimate targets.
President Trump praised those who were involved in making the arrests.
"It was an amazing job. We had them under investigation. They were looking to do big damage to our fort. And working with the British worked out great," he told reporters in Chicago on Sunday. "We had them under view for a long time and we got them."
Iran says it is ready for either diplomacy, or a return to fighting as war reaches 7-month mark
Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Sunday that Tehran was ready for either diplomacy or a return to fighting in the war sparked seven months ago by joint U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran. He said it is now up to President Trump to choose which direction to go.
"We are fully prepared for the time for the war to be resumed, and I repeat, we stand firm in the face of any new aggression, even if it comes to a doomsday war," Araghchi told NBC News' "Meet the Press."
"At the same time, we stand ready for diplomacy. It is up to President Trump to choose," he said.
President Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's proposal to return to a ceasefire agreement that collapsed months ago as part of a seven-day plan that would see it reopen the Strait of Hormuz to commercial shipping.
Araghchi said Tehran would wait for an official response from mediators.
Trump expects talks with Iran to resume this week
President Trump said Sunday that he expects talks with Iran to resume in the coming week, a day after he rejected a truce proposal put forward by Tehran.
"They want to make a deal, but it is not the deal that I want to make," Mr. Trump told Axios in a phone interview on Sunday. "It is what we would have maybe agreed to a year ago."
Iran said Friday it had submitted a proposal to the U.S. to reopen the Strait of Hormuz over seven days, but Mr. Trump asserted that Iranian leaders wanted the deal because "they are losing so badly."
"They overplayed their hand," Mr. Trump told Axios.
The president said resuming strikes on Iran was not off the table, adding: "I am always thinking about it."
CBS/AFP
Sen. Kennedy says Iran's plan was "not a serious offer"
Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana said Iran's proposed plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart talks was "not a serious offer."
"The president's not Bambi's baby brother. He turned it down," Kennedy said Sunday on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."
"We need to continue doing what we're doing — the sanctions, the blockade," said Kennedy.
"Now there's just one problem: The strait is at least partially closed, and it's affected the price of oil. And oil's in everything, including gasoline, and it's painful as hell," he said, adding: "We've got to either figure out a way to settle this thing, to get the strait open, or to escalate."
Kennedy said he would not support sending U.S. ground troops into Iran, however.

articles.title: South Korea eyes Turkish engines for its drones
articles.body:
- South Korea's Defense Acquisition Program Administration asked TAI about buying TEI's PD170 drone engine, which powers Türkiye's Anka and Aksungur drones.
- The inquiry follows two failed Korean military drone demonstrations in August and September, including kamikaze drones that crashed seconds after launch.
South Korea’s arms procurement agency has asked Türkiye whether it can buy the Turkish PD170 drone engine, a powerplant already flying on some of the world’s most combat-tested drones, as Korean military drone programs suffer a string of public crashes.
Turkish Aerospace Industries, or TAI, recently received an inquiry from South Korea’s Defense Acquisition Program Administration about buying the PD170 turbodiesel engine built by its subsidiary TEI, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency reported Sept. 27. A TAI official told Yonhap the company views potential cooperation with South Korea broadly and hopes joint engineering projects could lay the groundwork for long-term industrial partnerships and new aerospace programs.
Neither side has said which Korean drone program the engines would power, how many Seoul wants or what a deal might be worth. An official at Türkiye’s defense procurement agency, SSB, told Yonhap he could not comment on specific engine models and that a statement would come only after the necessary procedures and negotiations are finished.
The PD170 is a 170-horsepower turbodiesel built for medium-altitude, long-endurance drones, the fixed-wing aircraft that fly for a day or more to watch or strike targets. It powers TAI’s Anka and Aksungur drones and, according to Yonhap, Baykar’s Bayraktar TB2 and TB3. TAI said an Aksungur fitted with the engine stayed aloft for 45 hours and reached 42,000 feet (12,800 m). TEI says the design draws on experience from building engines for U.S.-designed F-16 fighter jets under license in Türkiye.
Turkish drones have been used in combat in Ukraine and across the Middle East, and Türkiye’s defense exports passed $10 billion last year. TAI has also been pushing into more advanced designs. Last month, it said its Anka-3 stealth drone launched two Süper Şimşek jet-powered drones from under its wings during a test flight. Yonhap reported the idea is for the small drones to mimic larger aircraft, draw fire from enemy air defenses and expose their radars, which the Anka-3 could then attack. The Anka-3 originally flew with a Ukrainian engine, and TEI’s own TF6000 turbofan is now being integrated into the aircraft.
South Korea has become one of the world’s fastest-growing arms exporters, with Chunmoo rocket launchers sold to Croatia, K2 tanks certified under NATO’s quality assurance system and rising Middle Eastern interest in its Cheongung-II air defense missiles. Its military drones have had a harder year.
On Sept. 16, at the Ministry of National Defense’s 2026 defense drone technology exhibition, a jet-powered drone developed by Korea Aerospace Industries nosedived into the ground right after takeoff. On Aug. 25, the South Korean Navy and the Agency for Defense Development tried to launch medium-size kamikaze drones from the 14,500-ton amphibious assault ship ROKS Marado in waters south of Busan. Both drones flew for only a few seconds before falling into the sea, and the planned strike on an uncrewed surface vessel never happened. The Navy said it would keep testing the drones’ performance at sea.
Yonhap described the engine inquiry as linked to assessments that South Korea lags behind in drone technology, though neither Seoul nor Ankara has said that directly.

articles.title: Ukraine’s cheap Patriot rival now has a two-mode seeker
articles.body:
- Fire Point now lists the FP-7.x Freyja interceptor's seeker as combined infrared and radar, replacing the infrared-only seeker it described earlier.
- The company plans its first ballistic target interception with the missile around July 2027.
Ukrainian missile maker Fire Point has changed the published specifications of its FP-7.x anti-ballistic interceptor, now listing a combined infrared and radar seeker for the weapon instead of the infrared-only seeker it described earlier.
The company posted an updated specification card for the missile on X, which it calls the FP-7.x Freyja interceptor. In August, when co-founder and chief designer Denys Shtilerman presented the Freyja project, Fire Point said the interceptor would use an imaging infrared seeker, which homes in on a target’s heat signature. Fire Point did not explain the change or say who supplies the radar component.
A seeker is the sensor in a missile’s nose that finds the target and steers the weapon in the final seconds of flight. Pairing infrared and radar lets a missile use both a target’s heat and its radar reflection to track it, which can help when one sensor is degraded by weather, decoys or the target’s own design.
The card lists the FP-7.x as 7.25 m (23.8 feet) long and 0.53 m (21 inches) in diameter, with a top speed of 1,500 to 2,000 m/s, or roughly 5,400 to 7,200 km/h (3,400 to 4,500 mph). It carries a fragmentation warhead, which explodes near the target and sprays it with metal pieces. The missile flies on inertial guidance, using onboard sensors to track its own position, and receives course corrections by radio from the ground while in flight.
For comparison, Russia’s Iskander-M ballistic missile travels at about 2,100 m/s at the end of its powered flight, according to Fire Point’s August presentation.
The FP-7.x is the interceptor for Freyja, a pan-European project to build a cheaper ballistic missile defense system than the U.S.-made Patriot. Ukraine and nine other European countries signed a declaration launching the effort on July 13. Fire Point serves as the main system integrator and has signed agreements with 13 European defense companies, including Hensoldt, Thales, Diehl Defence, Saab, Kongsberg, Leonardo, MBDA and Safran, to supply radars, guidance, seekers and command-and-control equipment.
Fire Point is a Kyiv-based company founded in 2022 and is best known for its FP-1 long-range attack drones and FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. The FP-7.x is a faster version of the company’s FP-7 ground-attack ballistic missile, and Fire Point has said the FP-7’s initial design drew on Soviet-era S-300 and S-400 interceptor designs. The company says the airframe is built from composite materials to keep costs down.
Fire Point chief executive Iryna Terekh told Janes in July that the current FP-7.x uses a blast-fragmentation warhead, which gives a low chance of destroying an incoming ballistic missile’s payload, and that the company plans to develop it into a hit-to-kill interceptor that strikes the target directly. She said the missile’s top speed is expected to rise to about 2,200 m/s as the program matures.
The company wants each interceptor to cost less than €1 million ($1.14 million), about a quarter to a sixth of the reported price of a Patriot interceptor, and aims to produce 2,000 a year. Ukraine relies heavily on Patriot to stop Russian ballistic missiles, and global supplies of those interceptors are limited.
Fire Point has said it hopes to have its first FP-7.x interceptors ready by the end of 2026 if European partners deliver the components it still needs, and plans the first interception of a ballistic target around July 2027.

Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the drone struck Ukrainian territory around 2 kilometers (1.2 miles) from the Dorohusk crossing and did not enter Polish airspace.
The shelters will initially be installed at stations in densely populated areas and near major roads and will be available to anyone nearby, Ukrnafta CEO Bohdan Kukura said.
