articles.title: Trump denies Iran concessions in ‘hoax’ report
articles.body:
Trump denies Iran concessions in ‘hoax’ report
US President Donald Trump has denied offering any concessions to Iran after indirect negotiations resumed in New York on Monday in hopes of ending the war launched by the US and Israel against the Islamic Republic seven months ago.
Trump took to social media to refute an Axios report claiming that he was prepared to lift some sanctions and release frozen Iranian funds in return for “concrete Iranian steps” regarding its nuclear program. AP published similar claims early Tuesday morning, also citing US officials.
“This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING! Axios’ story, like most others, is a HOAX, used only for purposes of satisfying their Trump Derangement Syndrome,” he wrote on Truth Social, demanding that the “fake story” be taken down.
US and Iranian officials met separately with mediators on the sidelines and are expected to focus on a revised proposal submitted by Tehran last week during the UN General Assembly, according to Reuters.
Trump confirmed on Saturday that he had rejected Iran’s proposal for a seven-day ceasefire that would have reopened the Strait of Hormuz, arguing that he sought a better deal. The US president has emphasized that his primary goal is to dismantle Iran’s nuclear program and ensure that Tehran never acquires nuclear weapons.
Iran, meanwhile, has maintained that its nuclear program is entirely peaceful and that uranium enrichment is its right as a sovereign state.
The situation remains tense around the Strait of Hormuz, where disruptions to shipping are driving up energy prices worldwide. On Wednesday, an Indian sailor was killed after a projectile struck the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged cargo ship Cape Dao. Although Iran has not claimed responsibility for the attack, it has previously warned vessels passing through the strait not to use the “illegal” routes designated by the US Navy.

articles.title: ‘Science Became a Target’: Europe Condemns Russian Strikes on Kyiv Civilian Sites
articles.body:
European leaders and top diplomats rallied behind Ukraine after Russia’s latest attacks on Kyiv struck the National Academy of Sciences, a medical facility and other civilian sites, with officials accusing Moscow of targeting civilians, science and critical infrastructure.
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attack demonstrated that Ukraine’s scientific community had itself become a target.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Today, science became a target for Russia,” von der Leyen wrote on X.
“My heart goes out to the heroes searching for people trapped inside Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences. As well as to the families and loved ones of the victims of horrific attacks across the country.”
“We stand with them. And with all Ukrainians,” she added. “Europe is working harder than ever to strengthen Ukraine’s defence.”
The international condemnation followed a day of Russian strikes across Kyiv on Sept. 28 that killed two people and injured 26, according to Kyiv authorities.
The Academy building was among several civilian sites hit during the attacks. A pharmaceutical company and medical facility were also struck, while damage was reported across multiple districts of the capital.
France: Russia Is ‘Targeting Civilians and Knowledge’
France’s Embassy in Ukraine placed the attack on the Academy alongside previous Russian strikes on educational institutions in Kyiv.
Russia to Begin Additional Mobilization, Expand North Korean Troop Presence
“Schools, universities of Kyiv, and now the Academy of Sciences, struck in broad daylight, set ablaze, just steps from the Opera,” the embassy wrote on X.
“By targeting civilians and knowledge, Russia is pursuing its escalation of terror. This cruelty will not go unpunished. France stands alongside Ukraine.”
Austria: Attacks Are ‘Absolutely Appalling’
Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker highlighted both the strike on the Academy and the attack on a medical facility in central Kyiv.
“Russia’s attacks on Ukraine are absolutely appalling and must stop!” Stocker wrote on X.
“A clinic and the National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv’s city center have been hit, and there has been near-constant bombardment for days.”
“Deliberately targeting civilians and carrying out acts of terror against the civilian population is reprehensible and a violation of international law,” he added.
Norway: ‘Civilian Institutions Must Not Be Targets’
Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide also singled out the National Academy strike.
“I am appalled by Russia’s latest attacks across Ukraine, including on the National Academy of Sciences in Kyiv,” Eide wrote on X.
“Scientists and staff should be able to work safely. Civilian institutions must not be targets of attacks. Norway stands firmly with Ukraine.”
Spain: Attacks Violate International Humanitarian Law
Spanish Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares accused Russia of continuing to strike civilian targets. Spain’s Foreign Ministry identifies Albares as the country’s current minister for foreign affairs, European Union and cooperation.
“I firmly condemn the continued attacks by Russia against civilian targets in Ukraine, in clear violation of international humanitarian law,” Albares wrote on X.
Lithuania Warns of ‘Reckless Escalation’
Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys went beyond the Kyiv strikes, warning about attacks near Ukraine’s border with Poland and routes used for international assistance.
“Strongly condemn Russia’s latest attacks against Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities, hitting the National Academy of Sciences, hospitals, and civilian infrastructure,” Budrys wrote on X.
He described Russian attacks near the Polish-Ukrainian border and along critical international assistance routes as “a reckless act of escalation.”
“Efforts to intimidate Ukraine and obstruct support are doomed to fail,” he said. “They will not weaken our resolve – we will continue supporting Ukraine and strengthening the pressure on Russia.”
Academy Strike Draws Particular Outrage
The National Academy of Sciences strike carried additional symbolic weight because the institution sits at the center of Ukraine’s scientific and academic establishment.
The attack caused a fire and prompted a rescue operation inside the building. Early reports from Kyiv authorities said one person had been killed and several others injured at the Academy site.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said emergency crews were searching for people who might still be trapped inside, stressing that the Academy was only one of several civilian sites struck across Ukraine that day.
“Every Russian act of terror results in casualties that could have been prevented if pressure on Russia had finally become total – pressure on everything that finances and produces Russia’s weapons of terror, and on everyone who uses them,” Zelensky said.
“The world must understand that terrorists will keep going if they are not stopped here, in Ukraine.”
“And such brutal strikes must not be ignored. There must be a response – with global resolve and strength.”
“We are counting on the strength of Europe, America, and our other partners who can help protect lives.”

articles.title: What is known about arrests at US airbase in Britain
articles.body:
Suspected plot to attack UK's Fairford airbase, used by US: What do we know?
LONDON, Sept 28 - British police said on Monday they were investigating whether individuals acting for a foreign state were involved in an apparent plot to attack an airbase used by the United States, but said five men they had arrested would be released on bail.
Below is what is known so far about the incident at RAF Fairford:
WHAT HAPPENED AT FAIRFORD?
Police were called to the airbase, 90 miles (145 km) west of London, early on Sunday morning by a local farmer who said she had seen three large white vans parked near the base and a group of "hooded and masked men" running into a field nearby.
Armed officers from the local force, Gloucestershire Police, responded and arrested five men in the Whelford area, about a mile from the base.
The five men were initially arrested on suspicion of offences under the explosives act and later on suspicion of preparation of a terrorist act after counter-terrorism police took over the investigation.
About 85 households were evacuated from properties near where the three vehicles were found and a 400-metre cordon was put in place around them.
WHY WERE THE MEN RELEASED?
The head of UK Counter Terrorism Policing, Laurence Taylor, said on Monday afternoon the men were being released after "extensive interviews and inquiries" and that they remained under investigation.
"They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others," he said.
He later said the incident was being considered from all angles, including whether offences had been committed "by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state."
WHAT DO WE KNOW ABOUT THE MEN WHO WERE ARRESTED?
The five men detained were all British nationals aged between 23 and 25 who lived in London, police said.
An image on social media purported to show some of the suspects, seated shirtless with hands behind their backs, after their arrest. Reuters was unable to independently locate and verify the source of the photograph.
WHY WOULD FAIRFORD BE A TARGET?
Fairford, which opened in 1944 and was used by allied troops for the D-Day invasion of Normandy, has this year been used by US forces for strikes on Iran.
It is one of the US Air Force's only European airfields suitable for heavy bombers, and played a key role in both the first Gulf War in 1991 and the invasion of Iraq in 2003.
Britain said in July its armed forces were ready to protect Fairford after Iran's Revolutionary Guards warned it not to allow US bombers to fly from the base. The Guards said any base used to launch attacks would be a legitimate target.
Over the last six weeks there has been increased surveillance in the area after a specific threat from the Iranians, according to a local councillor.
WHAT HAVE PEOPLE SAID SO FAR ABOUT THE INCIDENT?
The farmer, who has not been named, told British media she saw eight to 10 men running from the vans with their faces covered and that they got within about 100 metres of the perimeter fence of the airbase.
"I just can't process how that base was on such high alert, and that the men were even there," she said, adding that a blockade had focused only on the main entrance.
"I'm really glad they ran away."
British Defence Minister Wes Streeting told BBC TV he was grateful to the witness but that she only had a "partial picture" of what had happened after she said she was "staggered" it had been left to a member of the public to report them despite the heightened threat.
US President Donald Trump said on Sunday the group had been under investigation as part of a long-running investigation. "We had them under view for a long time, and we got them," he said, adding that the suspects intended "big damage" to the base.
Iran's embassy in London said in a statement on Monday that it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations" about Tehran's possible involvement in the incident. REUTERS

articles.title: Taiwan’s history of trapping invaders
articles.body:
The Chinese idiom “closing the door to beat the dog” (關門打狗) has evolved from a rural proverb into a polarizing strategic metaphor.
While modern Taiwanese leaders reject its derogatory language, the core tactic — luring an enemy into enclosed terrain, sealing escape routes, and launching an inescapable attack — is deeply woven into Taiwan’s legacy of resistance. Over centuries, local forces have repeatedly used geography and strategic choke points to resist stronger adversaries.
The folk and architectural blueprint
In traditional courtyards, catching an aggressive dog required shutting the main gate first to trap the animal. This found a physical manifestation in traditional East Asian military architecture through the wengcheng (甕城), or barbican system — walled enclosures built outside fortress gates that trapped invading forces inside a lethal bottleneck.
In 1948, Mao Zedong formalized a similar concept into military doctrine during the Liaoshen Campaign to isolate Nationalist forces at the Jinzhou railway junction.
However, long before and after Mao’s maneuvers, people in Taiwan adapted similar forms of entrapment as tools for survival.
Pre-Japanese and colonial resistance
Because Taiwan’s geography consists of dense forests, mountains, and narrow valleys, local resistance forces often relied on terrain to neutralize better-equipped conventional armies.
During the Lin Shuang-wen Rebellion of 1787–1788, Lin’s rebel forces faced Qing troops sent to suppress the uprising. According to accounts of the campaign, rebel forces exploited difficult terrain and fortified mountain positions while resisting Qing advances.
During the 1895 Japanese invasion, local Hakka and Hoklo volunteer militias under Wu Tang-hsing used the rugged terrain around Baguashan in Changhua while confronting advancing Japanese forces.
The battle became one of the largest engagements of the 1895 resistance and a defining example of how terrain shaped the fighting.
The 1930 Wushe Rebellion offers another example. Seediq Indigenous fighters under Mona Rudao used the difficult Mahebo terrain, including narrow mountain routes and suspension bridges, against Japanese forces.
Resistance fighters cut at least one important suspension bridge during the uprising to slow the Japanese advance. Japanese forces eventually responded with overwhelming military force, including aircraft.
The authoritarian reversal and postwar defense
During the 228 Incident and subsequent White Terror era, the logic of containment was tragically turned inward by the KMT authoritarian state.
Security forces used martial law, arrests, searches, port controls, and large-scale security operations to suppress dissidents, intellectuals, activists, and others deemed threats to the regime.
Two years later, however, geographic containment played a very different role during the Battle of Guningtou on Kinmen.
Former Japanese Imperial Army General Nemoto Hiroshi secretly traveled to assist KMT forces fighting the Chinese Communists and later advised Taiwan’s military leadership.
During the battle, PLA troops landed on Kinmen but became separated from reinforcements as Taiwan’s defenders used armor, artillery, air power, and coastal defenses to destroy or disable landing craft and isolate the invading force.
After approximately three days of fighting, the PLA landing force was defeated. The battle halted the immediate Communist advance on Kinmen and became one of the defining military encounters of the early cross-strait confrontation.
Modern cross-strait rhetoric
Today, Beijing has revived the idiom during military encirclement exercises around Taiwan.
Chinese state media and military commentators have used “closing the door to beat the dog” to describe scenarios in which PLA forces seek to cut Taiwan off from external support while preventing forces on Taiwan from escaping.
Taiwanese commentators have also used the phrase in a different context to warn taishang against moving manufacturing operations to China, where attractive incentives can later give way to regulatory pressure or restrictions once businesses are deeply invested.
The phrase remains potent enough to trigger domestic controversy.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, then-Taipei Mayor Ko Wen-je (柯文哲) used “closing the door to beat the dog” to describe his containment strategy during a major outbreak associated with Huannan Market.
Ko said the strategy involved concentrating screening and vaccination efforts among the highly mobile market population. His choice of language nevertheless drew criticism for its blunt and dehumanizing imagery.
The modern Western reversal
More recently, the metaphor has been applied to US-China diplomacy.
A Liberty Times analysis published after the September Trump-Xi summit argued that Western democracies — particularly the United States under President Donald Trump — had effectively turned the concept back against Beijing.
Unlike the psychological deception of the classic “Empty Fort Stratagem” (空城計), which relies on bluffing an opponent, the article portrayed the summit as a structural form of containment.
Washington offered Xi Jinping a lavish welcome and the prestige of a White House state visit while continuing to maintain extensive economic and technological restrictions on China.
The underlying argument is that ceremonial engagement does not necessarily translate into strategic concession. Washington can offer diplomatic theater while continuing to constrain Beijing in areas such as advanced technology, trade, and artificial intelligence.
Taiwanese agency
Crucially, this geopolitical contest is not merely a game played between superpowers. Taiwan possesses its own historical and contemporary agency and continues to use asymmetric defense and strategic maneuvering to secure its sovereignty.
Today, one source of Taiwan’s leverage lies in its “silicon shield” — its central position in advanced semiconductor manufacturing through TSMC.
In a conflict, this technological dominance would not function as an absolute barrier. Instead, Taiwan’s semiconductor industry acts as a major global economic tripwire.
Any blockade or occupation that disrupted advanced chip production would impose enormous costs not only on Taiwan, but on China and the wider global economy.
Taiwan also faces genuine vulnerabilities in energy resilience and maritime supply lines. Its agency therefore lies in raising the economic, military, and political costs of coercion.
By modernizing asymmetric military capabilities, reinforcing civic infrastructure, and deepening global economic interdependence, Taiwan can make aggression increasingly costly while strengthening its own resilience.
The goal is not to recreate an ancient battlefield trap. It is to ensure that coercion or invasion presents Beijing with costs that outweigh any conceivable benefit, preserving Taiwan’s freedom and democratic system.

articles.title: Pope Leo urges Russia, Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end war
articles.body:
Pope Leo urges Russia, Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end war
ABOARD THE PAPAL FLIGHT - Pope Leo on Sept 28 urged Russia and Ukraine to sit down and discuss how to end their four-year war, hours after he had urged European leaders seeking to end conflicts to make concessions to achieve peace.
The first US pope also decried national leaders who he said are “beginning to speak about nuclear weapons and wars that are becoming ever more destructive,” addressing a press conference aboard his flight to Rome after a four-day trip to France.
Leo said the Catholic Church has an obligation to call for peace and respect of human life.
“The Church has a responsibility to promote these values, continually inviting leaders — from Russia and Ukraine, as well as other countries — to come together, sit down, engage in dialogue,” said the pope.
He said leaders must “seek ways to solve problems without continuing these wars, which no longer make sense.”
“This is not about being political or non-political, but there needs to be a voice that seeks to promote the values of human dignity, the importance of life, and the possibility of perhaps spending more on health and education and less on weapons,” said Leo.
Earlier on Sept 28, the pope said Europe must be willing to sacrifice some positions to achieve peace in a speech in Metz, France, where he laid out his clearest vision yet for the future of the continent. REUTERS

articles.title: Beyond melodrama: Khajepasha on war, childhood and duty of Iranian cinema
articles.body:
Beyond melodrama: Khajepasha on war, childhood and duty of Iranian cinema
TEHRAN- Iranian filmmaker Babak Khajepasha believes cinema should do more than portray suffering. For him, a film dealing with war, the death of children, or a social tragedy should leave audiences with questions rather than simply tears.
Khajepasha, whose “In the Arms of the Tree” was selected as Iran’s submission for the 2025 Academy Awards, has repeatedly turned to children and family in his films. His latest feature, “The Land of Angels”, deals with children in Gaza. The film has also taken part in international events, including the Altyn Minbar Kazan International Film Festival, where it received the Grand Prix for Best Feature Film. Khajepasha is also among the jury members of the 2026 BRICS+ International Film Festival in St. Petersburg.
In an interview with the Tehran Times, he spoke about the possibility of making a film on the recent tragedy in Minab, the difficulty of depicting the death of children without reducing cinema to melodrama, his decision to make films during the 40-day war, and what he saw during a recent visit to Hiroshima. He also discussed the international position of Iranian cinema, his earlier criticism of the Oscars and some major festivals, and why family remains one of the subjects he wants to pursue in his future work.
Looking beyond the tragedy
Speaking about the possibility of making a film about the tragedy in Minab, Khajepasha said he would be more interested in exploring the reasons behind such events than simply depicting their devastating consequences.
“The aspect that I, as a filmmaker, can enter and that deserves to be explored is the reason behind this tragedy,” he said, stressing that society should ask why it has been forced to experience such pain.
The filmmaker pointed to the loss of children in different parts of Iran, including Minab, Lamerd, Tabriz and Kermanshah during the recent war, saying that while addressing the suffering of children is important, cinema should also investigate why children repeatedly become victims of conflict and violence.
This concern, he explained, was also central to his research for “The Land of Angels”. During his research and conversations with Palestinians, he encountered stories that demonstrated the profound psychological impact of losing a child.
Khajepasha recalled speaking with a Palestinian father who had been holding his child when the child was killed. According to the filmmaker, the man later repeatedly returned to the same place, hoping that he too would be killed so that he could join his child. The father said he could not understand why he had been left alive.
For Khajepasha, such stories demonstrate that the killing of a child affects much more than the immediate victim. It leaves a psychological wound on the family and, ultimately, the wider community.
Yet he believes that cinema must be careful not to turn such suffering into an exercise in emotional manipulation.
From tears to questions
That is also why Khajepasha is wary of making films about war and children that rely entirely on emotion.
If simply seeing the suffering of children were enough to change the world's response to violence, he said, the many films and documentaries made about Gaza and other conflicts would already have brought about such a change.
“Just talking about how much pain we are in does not necessarily take us a step forward,” he said. “We have to look at this from an intellectual perspective. We have to search for its causes and ask where this pain is supposed to take us.”
For “The Land of Angels”, he wanted the audience to leave with a question.
A viewer may accept that there are fighters, a military conflict and casualties in a war, he explained. But the death of thousands of children should lead to another question: why are these children being killed?
That question, in his view, can open the door to wider discussions about the position of children in contemporary society, the pressures placed on them and even the declining importance attached to having children in some parts of the world.
Khajepasha prefers this kind of cinema to a film that simply asks its audience to cry.
“I don't want to make a film merely so that audiences cry,” he said. “We have to value the film itself. There have to be other reasons for making it.”
He pointed to techniques used in dramatic literature and epic theater, including distancing, which encourage audiences to think about a work instead of simply surrendering to its emotional effect. A film, he said, should stay with the viewer as a question after the screening.
When filmmaking becomes a duty
The same idea of responsibility was behind Khajepasha's decision to work during the 40-day War.
At the time, Tehran and other parts of the country were facing an extraordinary situation as they came under US and Zionist regime airstrikes. Khajepasha said he saw people from different professions doing more than their normal duties: bakers working additional shifts, doctors and nurses continuing their work in hospitals and other citizens finding ways to contribute.
For him and some of his colleagues, filmmaking became another form of service.
“Sometimes we make films because we are filmmakers. Sometimes, as Iranians, we have another national duty,” he said. “At that point, it is no longer simply about filmmaking. It is a form of service.”
Under ordinary circumstances, he acknowledged, starting a production so quickly and without the usual preparation would not have been logical. But he felt that the circumstances demanded a response.
“As someone working in the arts, I felt I had a responsibility,” he said. “My instrument is cinema and television.”
He began work only a few days after the war started and now looks back on the experience with particular satisfaction.
The reason, he explained, was not necessarily that the films were more successful than his other work. It was the feeling that he was doing something directly for his own people.
“I am happy that, during that period, instead of standing on the sidelines, I was able to take a step,” he said.
Hiroshima: between memory and spectacle
A recent trip to Hiroshima gave Khajepasha another opportunity to think about the way major human tragedies are remembered.
He attended the annual ceremony commemorating the victims of the atomic bombing of Hiroshima and found the gathering visually striking and, from a filmmaker's perspective, fascinating. Yet he said the event left him with mixed feelings.
The scale of the tragedy, he argued, seemed much greater than what was being conveyed by the ceremony.
“I felt that, instead of the truth being fully expressed, I was watching more of a show,” he said.
Khajepasha extended that observation to the way peace is sometimes represented internationally. He questioned the gap that can exist between institutions and governments that publicly promote peace and countries whose policies have contributed to conflicts elsewhere.
But his experience in Japan did not leave him simply pessimistic. He said he encountered ordinary people who appeared genuinely concerned about events beyond their own borders.
When some Japanese people learned that he was Iranian, he recalled, they immediately brought up the victims of the recent tragedy in Minab and other Iranian victims.
He said he had encountered similar reactions in other countries and believes that ordinary people may ultimately understand such tragedies more deeply than political rhetoric suggests.
Iranian cinema and the international festival circuit
Khajepasha also returned to comments he made while “In the Arms of the Tree” was Iran's Oscar submission. At the time, he had questioned whether artistic quality alone determines a film's international success.
His criticism, he explained, was not simply about whether his own film would advance in the Oscar race. He was talking about the broader position of art and cinema.
In his view, political considerations, lobbying and relationships can influence some major international cultural institutions. He also believes that the influence of politics has become particularly visible in some film festivals.
That does not mean he considers the entire international festival circuit politicized.
He mentioned festivals held in South Korea, Morocco, Egypt, Armenia, Russia and Turkey among festivals that continue to offer valuable platforms for filmmakers. Iranian cinema, he stressed, has also received genuine international recognition through films by directors such as Asghar Farhadi and Majid Majidi.
The quality of an individual film, he argued, should not be reduced to the festival at which it appears or the prize it receives.
“A festival award alone cannot determine the value of a film,” he said.
He also believes filmmakers themselves have a responsibility not to allow the desire for international recognition to dictate their artistic choices.
Family at the center
Children feature prominently in both “In the Arms of the Tree” and “The Land of Angels”, but Khajepasha does not see himself primarily as a filmmaker of children's stories.
His deeper interest, he said, is the family.
He usually tries to include children in his films because their presence gives the story another dimension, but he would like to explore the family itself more extensively in future work.
“I would like to make more films about the family itself,” he said, describing it as one of the most important and vulnerable foundations of human societies.
He believes the issue has particular importance in Iran because family relationships are deeply connected to the country's cultural identity.
Iran cannot simply reproduce changes that have taken place in other societies, he argued. Relationships among parents, children and extended family members have a particular cultural meaning in Iranian society.
For that reason, he believes Iranian cinema should address the pressures facing families instead of treating changes in family structures as inevitable.
‘First make a good film’
Khajepasha will soon have an opportunity to examine films from the other side of the filmmaking process, as a jury member of the BRICS+ International Film Festival in St. Petersburg.
At the time of the interview, the festival's films had not yet been sent to the jury, so he had not begun watching them. But he already knew what his first criterion would be.
The film itself comes first.
For Khajepasha, a film needs to have a sound story and plot as well as convincing cinematic elements such as mise-en-scène and visual language. A political or social message cannot make up for weaknesses in the filmmaking.
He is particularly critical of films that appear to have been made primarily to deliver a message.
“If we want to criticize a society, we first have to make a good film,” he said. “If we simply shout our message at the audience, the audience will realize immediately that the filmmaker has an agenda.”
The same principle applies to films carrying messages that he himself agrees with, he added.
“A good film that disagrees with our beliefs can sometimes be less damaging than a bad film that is trying to promote our beliefs,” he said.
As a juror, Khajepasha said his first priority would therefore be cinematic quality.
“Before a film can make an audience believe in its message, it has to make the audience believe in the film itself,” he concluded.
SAB/

articles.title: Turkmenistan Strengthens Its Air Defense With Chinese FK-2000 Systems
articles.body:
Turkmenistan publicly demonstrated for the first time the new Chinese FK-2000 anti-aircraft missile and artillery systems (AAMS) in service with the country.
The new systems were displayed during a military parade in Ashgabat marking the 35th anniversary of Turkmenistan’s independence.
Based on published footage of the parade, at least eight FK-2000s can be counted in the mechanized column. However, the official number of systems purchased by Turkmenistan has not yet been disclosed.
In an official Turkmen government statement, the FK-2000 was referred to as a system that was recently introduced into the country’s armed forces.
As the mechanized column passed by, the FK-2000s followed behind Chinese air defense systems that have been in service with Turkmenistan since 2016: the FM-90, KS-1A, and FD-2000.
The parade marked the first official confirmation of the FK-2000’s service with the Turkmen armed forces.
The FK-2000 is a Chinese self-propelled air defense missile system designed to destroy cruise missiles, high-precision air-to-ground munitions, air-to-ground missiles, unmanned aerial vehicles, and aircraft.
The system was publicly unveiled for the first time at the Airshow China international aerospace exhibition in Zhuhai in 2021.
The FK-2000 air defense missile system consists of a self-propelled air defense missile launcher on an 8×8 wheeled chassis, equipped with an unmanned combat turret.
The system can engage aircraft at ranges of 1.2 to 25 km and cruise missiles at ranges of 1.2-10 km.
The turret houses 12 anti-aircraft guided missiles with an independent elevation mechanism, while close-in air defense is provided by two 30-mm six-barrel cannons.
Also in January, these anti-aircraft systems were spotted in service with the Sudanese anti-government group Rapid Support Forces (RSF).

articles.title: Pentagon awards RTX's Raytheon $20.7 billion contract for AMRAAM missiles amid stockpile concerns
articles.body:
Pentagon awards RTX’s Raytheon $26.4 billion contract for AMRAAM missiles amid stockpile concerns
- The Pentagon awarded RTX’s Raytheon a $26.4 billion contract to speed up AMRAAM missile production amid concerns over depleted stockpiles from Middle East and Ukraine conflicts.
- AMRAAM missiles support air-to-air combat and air defence systems like NASAMS, used by the US and over a dozen allied countries, including Ukraine and Qatar.
- The deal aims to increase output as part of the "Arsenal of Freedom" initiative, with RTX planning to produce at least 1,900 missiles annually from 2026, pending Congressional funding.
AI generated
WASHINGTON - The Pentagon awarded RTX’s Raytheon business a provisional multiyear contract worth US$20.7 billion (S$26.44 billion) to accelerate production of AMRAAM missiles, as the military pushes to replenish stockpiles depleted by conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine.
The US has supplied large quantities of weapons to allies while also using munitions in its own military operations in Iran, raising concerns about inventories of key air defence and precision-guided weapons.
The AMRAAM is used in air-to-air jet fighter combat as well as in the National Advanced Surface-to-Air Missile System (NASAMS), which is used to defend the Washington area and is used by more than a dozen other countries, including Ukraine, Oman and Qatar.
The prospective AMRAAM deal is the latest in a series of large munitions contracts the Pentagon has pursued this year to pressure contractors into ramping output up faster.
The award follows a similar pattern to a US$58.6 billion Patriot interceptor deal awarded to Lockheed Martin in July, a seven-year procurement plan running through fiscal 2032.
As with that contract, industry executives have cautioned that Congress has not yet appropriated the funding needed to support the full multiyear commitment, meaning contractors may be unable to invest at scale in components and facilities until lawmakers act.
The production agreements are designed to entice contractors to move faster on increasing output, part of a broader push by the Trump administration to prioritise weapons production over shareholder returns.
The contract, if Congress ultimately appropriates the funds, would let RTX continue to invest in its workforce, supply chain and facilities as US demand surges.
The company said it nearly doubled AMRAAM production in 2025, compared with the prior year.
The deal would be part of the Pentagon’s “Arsenal of Freedom” initiative.
RTX said earlier in 2026 it would set an annual production goal of at least 1,900 AMRAAM missiles. REUTERS

articles.title: Taiwan tracks 9 Chinese ships, 3 military aircraft
articles.body:
TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of National Defense tracked three Chinese military aircraft, five naval vessels, and four official ships around Taiwan between 6 a.m. on Sunday and 6 a.m. on Monday.
One of the three People’s Liberation Army aircraft crossed the Taiwan Strait median line in the country’s northern air defense identification zone, according to the MND.
In response, Taiwan deployed aircraft, naval ships, and coastal-based missile systems to monitor PLA activity.
So far this month, the MND has tracked Chinese aircraft 220 times and ships 289 times. Since September 2020, China has increased its use of gray zone tactics by incrementally increasing the number of military aircraft and naval vessels operating around the country.
Gray zone tactics are defined as “an effort or series of efforts beyond steady-state deterrence and assurance that attempts to achieve one’s security objectives without resort to direct and sizable use of force.”

articles.title: Europe’s businesses are paying for Russia’s hybrid war
articles.body:
Police investigators work on the tarmac with a robot that is capable, among other things, of defusing explosives, near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany on Aug. 5, 2026. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images
Elisabeth Braw is a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, author of the award-winning “Goodbye Globalization” and a regular columnist for POLITICO. Her new book, “The Undersea War,” is out Oct. 8.
Plots against defense executives, a series of arson attacks against private companies and warehouses, and explosive drones at Germany’s Leipzig/Halle Airport.
Had any of these worked as intended, they would have caused immense damage, not to mention claimed lives.
Advertisement
This is the situation plaguing Europe today, faced as it is with a proliferation of gray-zone attacks. And while a definitive response from the continent is yet to materialize, the bloc has finally started to name and address the hybrid war it’s been pulled into. No, summits and statements won’t thwart attacks, but acknowledgement is famously the first step to recovery.
It was only a miracle that saved workers at Leipzig airport when, on Aug. 4, an approaching drone landed poorly and lost its load of explosives. Had things gone to plan, it would have exploded next to a Ukrainian Antonov plane ready for departure, causing immense damage to a busy airport servicing the people and businesses of large parts of Germany. (Investigators later found a second drone laden with military-grade explosives right next to the airport.)
But who would want to maim and kill airport users? On Sept. 1, the German government announced it had determined Russia was behind the attack.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt and Saxony’s Interior Minister Armin Schuster arrive for a news conference at Leipzig/Halle Airport on Aug. 5, 2026. | Jens Schlueter/Getty Images
Years ago, European governments would have preferred not to publicly attribute such reckless incidents because with attribution comes the need to respond. But this time Germany openly identified the Kremlin as the instigator, showing just how seriously Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s government is taking the incident.
That’s because the failed drone explosion is only the latest in a series of sinister activity of which Germany has been a particular target.
Just before the country’s national election in 2025, the exhaust pipes of hundreds of cars were sabotaged across the country, and stickers calling for people to vote for the Greens attached to their windows. While that last touch suggested environmental activists were behind the campaign, the perpetrators were later identified as agents working on Russia’s behalf.
Advertisement
A couple of months earlier, a parcel — which turned out to contain a bomb — caught fire at DHL’s depot at Leipzig/Halle Airport. The perpetrators of this event, too, were later found to be working for Russia. And a few months before that, German authorities uncovered a Russian assassination plot against arms manufacturer Rheinmetall’s CEO.
You all know about these cases, not just because I’ve written about them on these pages but because they were so brazen. And Germany is not the only country to see all manner of businesses — and even business executives — targeted by geopolitically linked strikes. The U.K. has been hit by arson, as have Poland, the Czech Republic and other European countries.
In September 2025, objects in the skies above airports in Denmark and Norway forced temporary closures. Drones keep appearing around Scottish offshore installations. Numerous Swedish communication masts have sustained suspicious damage. And in the Baltic Sea, there has been a string of suspicious cable and pipeline incidents.
The Eagle S oil tanker is escorted by a tugboat to the Port of Kilpilahti in the Gulf of Finland on Dec. 28, 2024. | Vesa Moilanen/Lehtikuva/AFP via Getty Images
So far, none of these incidents have caused devastating damage — though a 2024 arson attack subsequently attributed to Russia destroyed Poland’s largest shopping mall. But each attempt costs the affected businesses money. Each piece of sabotaged infrastructure incurs repair costs and operational losses. Each disruption causes delays and further expenses. In fact, most targeted companies have seen their operations disrupted, which means additional financial hits.
In the case of the undersea cables struck by anchors, the owners were left with significant repair bills. For power cables, repairs typically run into the tens of millions of euros. Each incident also costs personnel time. Had the Leipzig drones or parcel bombs exploded, the financial losses — and, of course, the human losses — would have been extremely painful.
Even a relatively small incident can leave the target facing significant damage: Last month WB Group, a Polish drone-component manufacturer, was subject to an arson attack and incurred losses of at least €3.5 million. Polish prosecutors believe the attack was, again, instigated by Russia.
Advertisement
But when all this happens, who foots the bill?
If the companies are lucky, their insurers will. However, standard insurance only covers standard perils. It doesn’t cover war-like acts, which is what geopolitically linked acts of harm amount to. At least that’s what many standard insurers are unsurprisingly contending. And while specialized war insurers do offer coverage for war, doing so involves having to decide what exactly constitutes war-like acts.
The most detailed discussion of this fundamental question isn’t taking place at think tanks or universities. They’re taking place in the insurance industry, as vast amounts of money are at stake. And this — rendering European companies’ operations financially unsustainable — may, in fact, be Russia’s objective.
Surveillance drone models from WB Group are displayed during MSPO International Defence Industry Exhibition in Kielce, Poland on Sept. 8, 2026. | Omar Marques/Getty Images
Credit to the German government for convening the Baltic Sea Security Summit in August to accelerate European nations’ response to a discreditable and dangerous form of geopolitical score-settling, and for calling the Kremlin out.
Now, how will these subversive attacks on European companies continue to unfold? You will have to find out without me, as this is my farewell as a columnist for POLITICO. It has been an immense pleasure and honor to have your company. Arrivederci!
POLITICO occasionally publishes opinion pieces from guest authors to offer our readers a range of perspectives on the intersection of power and politics. The views expressed are those of the authors and do not reflect the views of POLITICO.

articles.title: Iranian women take up arms amid US threats (VIDEO)
articles.body:
Iranian women take up arms amid US threats (VIDEO)
Iranian women have been flocking to Imam Hossein Square in central Tehran to receive basic military and first-aid training as part of the ‘Sacrifice for Iran’ popular campaign.
The training center was inaugurated there last Wednesday, with the commander of the Basij paramilitary force, Hojjatoleslam Hossein Taeb, attending the opening ceremony.
According to Iranian media, the movement emerged as a grassroots initiative in late March, at the height of the US-Israeli military campaign against the Islamic Republic. It is based on the concept of ‘popular defense,’ which traces its roots to the bloody Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s.
The number of civilian volunteers, including dozens of women, enrolling in the training course has risen recently amid renewed threats from US President Donald Trump, RT’s Saman Kojouri reports from Tehran.
Participants register online and first receive basic training in handling weapons, including firearms, small drones, and shoulder-fired anti-tank missiles, as well as in tactical medicine. Volunteers subsequently have the option to progress to more advanced training.

articles.title: Airmen, Guardians Told to Select Religion Code from New Consolidated List
articles.body:
Active-Duty Airmen and Guardians have until mid-October to update their personnel records with their religious preference using the Pentagon’s new consolidated list of Religious Affiliation Codes, according to a recent Department of the Air Force announcement.
The new list of codes—ordered by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth—slashed the number of religions specified in the Pentagon’s HR systems from more than 200 to roughly 30. Officials said in June that the consolidation was necessary to streamline the number of religious preferences for service members and shape the chaplain corps to support them.
The consolidation process collapsed roughly 170 denominations of Christianity down to 21 and includes widespread non-Christian religions such as Buddhism, Hindu, Islam, and Judaism, among other faiths. It removes Wicca, paganism, and other nontraditional faiths from the list, replacing them with an “Other Religious” category.
The department directs all Active-Duty members of the Air Force and Space Force to select their new Religious Affiliation Code in the Virtual Military Personnel Flight system and certify their record of emergency data is accurate by Oct. 16, the announcement states. Members of the Air Force Reserve and Air National Guard have until Nov. 9 to update their records.
“Transitioning to these standardized codes ensures our chaplain corps has the accurate demographic data they need to provide tailored resources and support to our service members, while continuing to respect their individual convictions,” Richard Anderson, assistant secretary of the Air Force for manpower and reserve affairs, said in the announcement.
Airmen and Guardians who fail to update their RAC before the deadline will have their records automatically updated to a selection that aligns with the new RAC list. For example, paganism would likely fall under the “Other Religions” category, according to an Air Force official.
Individual Airmen and Guardians, however, will not be limited by the new RAC list for the purposes of identifying their religious preference on the ID tags or “dog tags” they wear around their necks. The tags can be vital for helping chaplains determine the religious needs of service members wounded in battle.
Hegseth announced the effort to consolidate the list of religious preferences in a March 24 video on social media, calling the older list of Faith and Belief Codes “impractical and unusable.” Hegseth also directed chaplains to replace their rank insignia with their appropriate religious affiliation insignia in an effort to make them more approachable to younger service members. The announcement came six months after Hegseth singled out paganism in September 2025 because some troops have petitioned for religious exemptions so they could grow beards.
“If you want a beard, you can join Special Forces,” Heseth told hundreds of general officers at Quantico, Va., last Sept. 30. “If not, then shave. We don’t have a military full of Nordic pagans, but unfortunately, we have had leaders who either refuse to call BS and enforce standards, or leaders who felt like they were not allowed to enforce standards.”
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell has argued the new consolidated RAC list is not intended to provide a list of “officially approved” religions. Rather it is “designed to allow chaplains to quickly look at the religious composition of their units and determine how they structure resources to best provide for warfighters of all faith groups,” Parnell wrote in a June 5 social media post.

articles.title: Denmark buys Ukrainian-founded firm’s ground drones
articles.body:
- Denmark bought nine Dropla 4x4 unmanned ground vehicles to train drone operators, including conscripts, at the Danish Defence Drone Center.
- The vehicles were delivered without weapon mounts, and Denmark is studying adding remote weapon stations and communications equipment.
Denmark’s armed forces have taken delivery of nine unmanned ground vehicles built by Dropla, a Danish company founded by Ukrainians, to train drone operators, including conscripts, at the country’s military drone center.
Denmark’s defense procurement agency, known by its Danish initials FMI, bought the Dropla 4×4 vehicles for the Danish Defence Drone Center, the agency said Sept. 28. An unmanned ground vehicle, or UGV, is a vehicle that drives itself or is steered remotely with no crew aboard. The agency did not disclose the price of the order or when the vehicles arrived.
The Danish version of the Dropla 4×4 was delivered without a weapon mount. FMI said it is already studying how to fit the vehicles with extra equipment such as a remotely operated weapon station, which lets a soldier aim and fire a machine gun from a safe distance, and new communications gear. The agency said those plans draw on lessons from the war in Ukraine and on its own trials of other UGVs in Denmark.
Colonel Thomas Øgendahl Knudsen, who heads FMI’s land division, said unmanned systems are developing quickly, so the Danish military needs to build experience with them and bring them into soldier training now. He said the new vehicles let the drone center work with ground drones while exploring how the technology could be used across the armed forces in the future.
The purchase is FMI’s second batch of UGVs this year. Earlier in 2026, the agency bought eight unmanned ground vehicles for the Danish Army, which FMI said have since been tested in a range of operational scenarios with strong results.
Dropla Tech was founded in 2023 by four Ukrainian entrepreneurs and is headquartered in Odense, Denmark, with its engineering and operations teams working in Ukraine. The company is best known for Blue Eyes, an artificial intelligence system that detects mines, improvised explosive devices and loitering drones without needing a cloud connection. Dropla says the system has confirmed more than 5,000 explosive threats in Ukraine.
The company builds two modular UGV platforms, the Dropla 4×4 and Dropla 6×6. Both can be configured for casualty evacuation, cargo delivery, reconnaissance, remote weapon stations and counter-drone missions. Dropla has also signed an agreement with Ukrainian company Frontline Robotics to integrate its Burya weapon turret onto the vehicles.
The Danish military has worked with Dropla before. During a six-month innovation project that ended this summer, the armed forces tested a Dropla prototype built for evacuation and logistics. That vehicle started out with four wheels but was fitted with two more on the military’s recommendation to make it more stable.
Dropla raised €2.4 million ($2.7 million) in 2025 from investors including Denmark’s state Export and Investment Fund, and in July 2026 it received an undisclosed investment from U.S.-Ukrainian group MITS Capital. The company says it wants to scale production to as many as 3,000 UGVs a year.

articles.title: Iran nearing completion of key rail link key for India’s gateway to Eurasia
articles.body:
Iran nearing completion of key rail link key for India’s gateway to Eurasia
Iran has completed laying track on the southern stretch of the Chabahar-Zahedan railway, closing a key gap in a route designed to connect the port of Chabahar on the Gulf of Oman to Zahedan near the Afghan border. 
Iranian railway official Abbas Khatibi said last week that tracks had been laid for the crucial 480km stretch between Chabahar and Khash, and currently the priority is to complete the stations on the route, Tasnim news agency reported. 
The Chabahar–Zahedan link stretches 630 km, or 735 km including branch lines. With the northern sections already linked to the existing rail network, the Iranian authorities are now preparing it for operation. 
The Chabahar–Zahedan link is an extension of the larger International North–South Transport Corridor (INSTC), backed by India, Iran and Russia. The project has been in the making for decades because of its huge infrastructure requirements and has also been slowed by Western sanctions on both Iran and Russia. 
The milestone comes as the Middle East conflict has disrupted traditional transport and energy routes across the region. Chabahar has direct access to the Indian Ocean without requiring ships to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, a major chokepoint affected by the conflict.
Strategic Step: Iran Completes Chabahar-Zahedan Rail Link – Connecting Central Asia to Indian Ocean
The major infrastructure project looks set to become fully operational within 3-4 months with final safety checks for the route underway. (Economic Times)
The route connects… pic.twitter.com/pUKsSzJEJq
For India, the Chabahar-Zahedan link strengthens a trade route that reaches Afghanistan and Central Asia without transiting Pakistan. Cargo arriving by sea at Chabahar would be able to move inland through Iran’s rail and road network toward landlocked regional markets. 
India’s role in Chabahar is complicated by US sanctions. A conditional waiver covering the project, in which India invested around $120 million, expired in April. New Delhi maintained it was discussing the issue with both Tehran and Washington, describing the regional conflict as a “complicating factor.” 
In July, the conflict touched Chabahar itself, when US forces struck a surveillance tower at the neighboring Shahid Kalantari terminal linked to the project. India said the terminal was not damaged.

articles.title: Trump's Taxpayer-Funded Ads Draw Bipartisan Criticism
articles.body:
President Donald Trump declares that “this is the final battle” in one of several taxpayer-funded television ads airing ahead of November’s midterm elections, prompting bipartisan scrutiny over whether the spots violate federal law.
The 30-second ad is a black-and-white video of Trump walking down a hall over audio of his warnings against “the deep state,” “warmongers,” “globalists,” “Marxists,” “communists,” and “fascists.”
Trump posted the same video on his Truth Social platform in 2023, but with one difference: Then, the monochromatic ad ended with words on screen calling on the viewer to join Trump’s campaign and fine print saying it was “Paid for by Donald J. Trump for President 2024, Inc.” This time, the 2026 ad says at the bottom: “Paid for by the U.S. Government.”
CNN reported that the ad aired during at least two NFL games on Sunday. CNBC also reported that the ad aired during Fox News Sunday, citing data from advertising intelligence company AdImpact, adding that the TV ad has cost more than $362,000 so far.
A second advert with the same “paid for by the U.S. government” disclaimer began airing on Wednesday. The ad, which featured the song “Love Me” by singer-songwriter JMSN, showed a montage of photos and videos of Trump, intercut with campaign talking points like “largest tax cuts in history” and “reigniting American manufacturing.” This ad, which CNBC reported also aired over the weekend, citing AdImpact data, has cost the federal government nearly $920,000 to date. It also apparently did not get the approval of JMSN, who posted on social media that he “would never authorize my music to be used for ANY political agenda or campaign.”
A third, which is a minute long, features scenic views of Mount Rushmore interspersed with parts of Trump’s speech there for the Fourth of July anniversary.
The ads appear to be part of a campaign blitz ahead of the November midterms, in which the GOP is hoping to defend its majorities in Congress.
Some lawmakers, including from his own Republican Party, are raising concerns with Trump and the White House over the advertisements. Asked about the ads by CBS News on Sunday, Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana said: “I don’t think any public official, including President Trump or Kristi Noem or John Kennedy, should spend public money on private ads for themselves.” (Kennedy was referring to former Homeland Security Secretary Noem, who came under fire for spending $220 million on an advertising campaign for border security.)
When asked about the “Love Me” ad, Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina said that the use of taxpayer money was reminiscent of the far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. “It’s inappropriate,” Tillis told reporters.
Rep. Thomas Massie, a Kentucky Republican and a vocal Trump critic, posted on social media about the “Final Battle” ad: “Don’t worry, using taxpayer dollars to run ominous campaign ads of the President has been done before and is completely legal… in banana republics.”
Democrats also raised questions. In a Sept. 24 letter to White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, Sen. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire demanded answers on the “Love Me” ad’s production cost, the agencies and external contractors involved, the source of funds, and the legal and ethical bases for the spot. Hassan wrote in her letter that the ad “does not have a clear official government purpose and appears to run afoul of federal prohibitions.” Sen. Andy Kim of New Jersey posted to social media about the black-and-white clip: “How much taxpayer money did the government spend on this ad?”
In another Sept. 24 letter, congressional Democrats on appropriations panels wrote to the White House that the “Love Me” ad should be taken off the air, as it was “the sort of government propaganda one might expect in North Korea, not the United States of America, and it is an egregious and illegal misuse of Americans’ hard-earned tax dollars.”
But the White House has defended the ads—which it called, in a Sept. 25 press release, “public service announcements.” A White House official told TIME Thursday that the ads weren’t political, didn’t have a call to action, and that the President wasn't on the ballot.
A spokesperson instead said that the ads were “about reminding Americans to love their country and understand what makes it worth defending, at home, at our borders, and abroad.”
What does the law say?
Since the 1950s, yearly funding bills—including the appropriations measure the President recently signed—routinely ban the use of taxpayer funds for “publicity or propaganda.”
The Government Accountability Office, which investigates how appropriated funds are spent, has interpreted this to refer to material that is “purely partisan,” “self-aggrandizing,” or “covert.” But it also noted that administrations may need to advocate or defend their policies.
Some lawmakers have pointed to potential violations of the Hatch Act, the 1939 act that limits the political activities of federal civilian employees in the executive branch. The President is exempt from the Hatch Act, though some argue that White House employees who facilitated the airing of the ads aren’t. Last week, the non-profit advocacy group Public Citizen filed a complaint before the GAO and the Office of Special Counsel, which is responsible for overseeing Hatch Act violations, seeking investigation and enforcement of relevant laws.
In defense of the “public service announcements,” the White House has pointed to previous ad campaigns during the administrations of George W. Bush, Barack Obama, and Joe Biden. (During the Bush Administration, one campaign did violate the anti-propaganda measure.)
“When prior Administrations utilized the airwaves, it was called ‘public education,’” the Trump White House said. “When this Administration promotes pride in our country, many of those same voices call it ‘propaganda.’”

articles.title: Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight: an administrative building and an educational institution were damaged
articles.body:
Russia struck Kyiv with ballistic missiles overnight: an administrative building and an educational institution were damaged
Kyiv • UNN
In Kyiv, missile debris damaged an administrative building and an educational institution, while a non-residential structure caught fire in the Pecherskyi district. Twenty-six people have been affected by the attacks since September 28.
On the night of September 29, Russian forces attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles, causing damage in the capital's Solomianskyi and Pecherskyi districts. Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported the consequences of the attack, UNN writes.
Details
In the Solomianskyi district, missile fragments fell in the courtyard of a residential building. Hits were also recorded on an administrative building of an infrastructure facility and an educational institution.
In the Pecherskyi district, a non-residential building caught fire as a result of the attack. Reports also emerged of a drone falling in the capital's government quarter, but there is currently no official confirmation of this information.
Attacks on Kyiv have continued since September 28
Earlier, Russian forces attacked the building of the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine. Two people were killed in the strike, including an aide to former Secretary of the National Security and Defense Council Volodymyr Horbulin. Horbulin himself was injured.
According to Klitschko, 26 people were injured as a result of Russian attacks on the capital, which continued from the morning of September 28. Eight of them were hospitalized.

articles.title: Putin restricts publication of Russian refinery, energy data amid Ukrainian strikes
articles.body:
Putin restricts publication of Russian refinery, energy data amid Ukrainian strikes
Russian President Vladimir Putin signed a decree on Sept. 28 restricting access to data on the country's oil refineries and energy exports amid an intensifying Ukrainian campaign against Russia's oil infrastructure.
The decree, published on Russia's official legal information portal, restricts access to information on the volume of oil processed and products manufactured by individual Russian refineries.
It also covers a broad range of information related to Russian energy exports, including the refined product slate, export quantities, pricing, and the supply chain of sellers, buyers, and intermediaries, as well as transportation routes, terminals, and storage locations.
Information concerning vehicles used for transportation of raw materials and exports, delivery dates and export operations is also included in the restrictions.
The decree prohibits dissemination of the restricted information through the media or online unless it has been disclosed by the company involved.
Relevant customs data will also be restricted.
Putin gave the Russian government a 10-day deadline to determine which specific products will be subject to the restrictions.
Reuters reported that the decree is intended to make Western sanctions against Russia more difficult to enforce.
Limiting the dissemination of information on export volumes, buyers, transport routes and terminals can make it more difficult for governments and researchers to track Russian energy flows and identify potential sanctions evasion.
Russia has previously restricted access to energy-sector information, including crude oil production data, as Western sanctions targeting the country's energy industry have expanded since Russia's illegal annexation of Crimea in 2014 and the beginning of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Reuters reported.
The latest restrictions come as Ukraine has intensified long-range attacks against Russian oil infrastructure, targeting refineries, depots and other facilities that Kyiv says support Moscow's war effort.
Ukraine's General Staff said on Sept. 21 that repeated Ukrainian long-range strikes had knocked out 45% of Russia's total oil refining capacity. The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the figure.
A fire was reported at the Pavlovskaya oil depot in Russia's Krasnodar Krai overnight on Sept. 28 amid a large-scale drone attack on the region.
Two days earlier, Ukrainian forces struck the Ilsky oil refinery elsewhere in Krasnodar Krai, sparking a fire at the facility. Ukraine's General Staff later confirmed the attack.

articles.title: Liminal’s mass-producible UGV heads to Pentagon trial
articles.body:
- Liminal Industries advanced to Phase II of GroundBreaker 1 and will demonstrate its DUEL-V unmanned ground vehicle at Camp Grafton, North Dakota, in mid-October.
- Companies that perform well may be invited to propose for a prototype Other Transaction Agreement award.
Liminal Industries, a U.S. startup building unmanned ground vehicles meant to be produced and fielded in large numbers, has advanced to the second phase of the GroundBreaker 1 competition and will demonstrate its DUEL-V vehicle to U.S. military evaluators in North Dakota next month.
The company announced Sept. 28 that its Phase I submission passed technical evaluation and that it will bring multiple DUEL-V vehicles to Camp Grafton in mid-October. An unmanned ground vehicle, or UGV, is a vehicle that operates on land with no crew aboard, driven by a remote operator or by its own software.
DUEL-V, short for Dynamic Unmanned Expendable Light Vehicle, is a compact, remotely operated platform that Liminal designed around three priorities: low cost, adaptability and the ability to build it at scale. It uses a modular layout that accepts different mission payloads, runs on four-wheel drive and can operate in either orientation. The company has not released its size, weight, speed, range, payload capacity or price.
“Scale has been a design requirement from the beginning,” said Bradley Balzer, founder and CEO of Liminal Industries. “Cost, manufacturing, and operator usability determine whether a ground system can become a widely deployed capability. GroundBreaker gives us an opportunity to demonstrate that approach and put DUEL-V in front of the people who will shape its deployment at scale.”
Liminal says its development relies on field testing, feedback from operators and rapid hardware changes between versions. It first unveiled DUEL-V on Oct. 14, 2025, when Balzer pitched it as the ground equivalent of an FPV drone, the cheap first-person-view quadcopters that armies in Ukraine now use by the hundreds of thousands. At the time, the company did not disclose payload options, how much the vehicle can drive itself or whether it can keep working under electronic jamming, and it has not released those details since.
GroundBreaker 1 is a joint Department of War demonstration meant to speed up the military’s adoption of unmanned ground vehicles. U.S. Army Contracting Command issued the call for white papers on Aug. 21 through the Department of War Drone OTA Consortium, which limited the competition to companies already enrolled in that consortium. Government teams from the Office of the Secretary of War and the military services are supporting the event.
The U.S. Army is looking for complete systems that troops can use in both combat and non-combat settings. The solicitation lists missions including reconnaissance and surveillance, tactical logistics, explosive ordnance disposal and route clearance, search and rescue, and force protection. White papers were scored out of 100 points: 40% for technical merit and design, 35% for readiness to deliver and demonstrate, 15% for cost and affordability, and 10% for past performance. The recommended threshold to reach Phase II was 75 points.
At Camp Grafton, service members will operate the vehicles in realistic field conditions and give feedback on how easy they are to use and how well they perform their missions. Companies will also make live pitches to government evaluators. Vendors whose vehicles show “high tactical value and technical maturity” may then be invited to submit a full technical and cost proposal for a prototype Other Transaction Agreement, a contract type the Pentagon uses to buy and test new technology faster than through traditional procurement.
GroundBreaker follows the demonstration-first model of the Department of War’s Drone Dominance Program, which runs aerial drones through competitive “Gauntlet” trials before placing large orders. The department has not said how many UGVs it plans to buy after GroundBreaker 1 or how many companies will take part in the October event.

articles.title: Russian Mobile Air Defense Teams Likely Armed with Chinese QW-18/19 MANPADS
articles.body:
Russian mobile air defense teams are likely armed with Chinese QW-18/19 man-portable air defense systems.
This is evidenced by footage from Russian television published by X user TheDeadDistrict.
The system was shown during an exercise with a mobile air defense team from Russia’s 51st Air Defense Division in the Rostov region.
During a conversation with the servicemen, the system was referred to as “Iva.” However, it does not resemble any MANPADS currently in Russian service.
The weapon’s appearance suggests similarities to the Iranian Misagh-3 and Chinese QW-18A/QW-19 MANPADS.
A detailed analysis of the photo may indicate greater similarity to the Chinese MANPADS due to the presence of an additional element in the launcher’s nose section.
This protruding element is absent from available photos of the Iranian Misagh-3. These could be newer versions of the system; however, no photos show this particular placement of the element.
It is difficult to determine the exact model of the Chinese system — QW-18 or QW-19. The MANPADS may also be supplied through Iran, as the country procures Chinese weapons, including MANPADS.
In July 2026, it was reported that Iran’s deal with China includes the delivery of up to 400 MANPADS, including QW-12 and FN-16 systems. The order is estimated to be worth $60–70 million.
In addition, Iran’s Misagh systems are based on Chinese QW-series MANPADS. Pakistan also produces similar systems under the designation Anza-2.
The use of foreign-made MANPADS may indicate that Russia’s defense industry is unable to meet the military’s demand and produce such systems in sufficient quantities.
Militarnyi previously reported that Ukraine had received confirmation that China was supplying weapons to the Russian Federation. This includes propellant and artillery systems.
Ukrainian intelligence agencies believe Russian-Chinese military cooperation also includes producing Chinese weapons in Russia.
